back: The ratio of the p.d. across a component to the current in it: R = V/I.
The resistance through which 1 A flows when the p.d. is 1 V (1 Ω = 1 V A⁻¹).
Current in a conductor is directly proportional to the p.d. across it, provided temperature and other physical conditions stay constant.

front: I-V graph of a filament lamp
back: Curve through the origin, symmetric, gradient decreasing as |V| rises: resistance increases as the filament heats.

front: I-V graph of a silicon diode
back: Negligible current in reverse bias and below about 0.6 V; rises very steeply above 0.6-0.7 V in forward bias.
Resistance falls as light intensity rises (light frees more charge carriers).
Resistance falls as temperature rises (heating frees more charge carriers).
Use V/I at the point, not the gradient (they agree only for an ohmic conductor).
Ammeter in series, voltmeter across the component, potential divider to vary V from zero, reverse connections for negative V.
